title: Shravan Kumar
hook: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes the picture of serving your parents
carry: honor mother and father as gods
tomorrow: what does a bad dream tell Bharata?

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, amends begin with telling the truth. You too will die grieving for a son, the blind father said. The truth spared the prince that night, but not the curse.

In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana. In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture: a son carrying his blind parents on pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders. Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. Here's the surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man has no name, and there are no baskets. Both came later.
screen: `A NAME CHILDREN KNOW.` → `TWO BASKETS ON A POLE.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing; he can't see her anymore. If only Rama would come back and touch me now, he says. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning the attendants come to wake him and find him gone. No son is there for the last rites: Rama is in the forest, and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom. So the ministers lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata comes, and send riders to Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing. Just bring him. Now the boy at the river. Valmiki calls him simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son. Later retellings call him Shravan Kumar and add the pilgrimage, his blind parents carried in two baskets on a pole. Why did a boy with no name become a children's story told across much of India? Because he carries a teaching Hindus hold close. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives a student leaving his teacher these parting words: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you. Caring for your parents, especially as they grow old, isn't only kindness in Hinduism. It's a sacred duty, close to worship. That's why grandparents tell this story at bedtime, and why calling someone a Shravan Kumar is high praise. Even the name fits: shravana is connected with hearing, and this boy was killed by an archer who shot at a sound.
screen: `THE KING DIES PAST MIDNIGHT.` · `A BODY KEPT IN OIL FOR BHARATA.` · `LATER: SHRAVAN KUMAR, AND THE BASKETS.` · `MATRU DEVO BHAVA. PITRU DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `HONOR MOTHER AND FATHER AS GODS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone older who looked after you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, or anyone who once carried something for you, and notice one specific thing they did: a meal, a ride, a hand on your shoulder. Let your breath stay with that picture, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer.
Shravana, hearing, the name later tellings give the boy at the river. Dasharatha dies grieving for his son, as that boy's father said he would.
Your line: honor mother and father as gods. That's what the boy with the baskets stands for. Day five hundred forty-four, done.

howItsDone: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

chat.meaning: Valmiki's hermit's son fetched water for his blind parents; later tellings named him Shravan Kumar. Hindus use the name for anyone who serves their elders, as the Upanishad says: let your mother and father be gods to you.
